correct_citation: Wu, H., Guo, Y., Yang, Y., Zhao, L., & Guo, C. (2021). A meta-analysis of the longitudinal relationship between academic self-concept and academic achievement. Educational Psychology Review, 33(4), 1749-1778.
design: Meta-analysis of 68 longitudinal studies (240 effect sizes); cross-lagged paths controlling for initial level of the outcome (prior achievement / prior self-concept)
population_location: Students across 68 longitudinal studies; location not stated in abstract
effect_as_reported: Achievement -> later ASC beta = 0.16; ASC -> later achievement beta = 0.08 (both p < .01); moderated by age, achievement level, measure type
excerpt: achievement significantly predicted ASC ([beta] = 0.16, p < 0.01) and vice-versa ([beta] = 0.08, p < 0.01) after controlling for the initial level of outcome variables
note: Authors, title, journal, year confirmed via ERIC; volume/issue/pages not confirmed from fetched text. Sorjonen et al. 2024 (B-005) disputes the reciprocal interpretation of this kind of baseline-adjusted estimate.

correct_citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., & Lüdtke, O. (2022). Directional ordering of self-concept, school grades, and standardized tests over five years: New tripartite models juxtaposing within- and between-person perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 34(4), 2697-2744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09662-9
design: Longitudinal panel, five waves; CLPM and RI-CLPM cross-lagged models (autoregressive, so prior achievement controlled); covariates gender and primary-school math and verbal achievement
population_location: N = 3,425 students over five years of compulsory secondary schooling (country not stated in abstract)
outcome: Math self-concept, school grades, standardized achievement tests
effect_as_reported: Consistent support for reciprocal (bidirectional) effects across CLPM and RI-CLPM; no coefficients in abstract
excerpt: lag-2 paths between non-adjacent waves; and covariates (gender, primary-school math and verbal achievement). Across all basic and extended RI-CLPMs and CLPMs, there was consistent support for the REM bidirectional-ordering hypothesis
note: Claim also holds for school grades, not only tests. Pages 2697-2744 from Crossref.

correct_citation: Talsma, K., Schüz, B., Schwarzer, R., & Norris, K. (2018). I believe, therefore I achieve (and vice versa): A meta-analytic cross-lagged panel analysis of self-efficacy and academic performance. Learning and Individual Differences, 61, 136-150. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.11.015
design: Systematic review and meta-analytic cross-lagged path analysis of two-wave longitudinal studies (pooled correlations; autoregressive paths control prior level)
population_location: k = 11 studies, N = 2,688; children and adults; location not stated
effect_as_reported: Performance -> later self-efficacy beta = 0.205; self-efficacy -> later performance beta = 0.071 (both p < .001); reciprocity for adults, not children
excerpt: Performance had a net positive effect on subsequent self-efficacy (β = 0.205, p < 0.001), significantly larger than the effect of self-efficacy on performance (β = 0.071, p < 0.001).
note: Abstract also says: in children performance uniquely impacts subsequent self-efficacy, but not the reverse. Small k (11). Pages 136-150 from OpenAlex.

correct_citation: Sorjonen, K., Ingre, M., Melin, B., & Nilsonne, G. (2024). Questioning the reciprocal effects model of academic self-concept and achievement: A reanalysis of a meta-analysis of longitudinal studies and a simulation. SAGE Open, 14(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/21582440241292826
design: Methodological reanalysis of a published meta-analysis plus simulation; no new data
population_location: Not applicable (reanalysis of meta-analytic estimates; simulated data)
outcome: Academic self-concept and achievement (methodological critique of baseline-adjusted prospective effects)
effect_as_reported: Different plausible models support opposing claims; true prospective effects not necessary for observed meta-analytic associations
excerpt: prospective effects were estimated while adjusting for a prior measurement of the outcome, and this method is susceptible to spurious findings due to correlations with residuals and regression to the mean
note: Abstract names 'a recent meta-analysis' without naming it here; proposes an extended skill development model as alternative. A critique, not evidence of an effect.

correct_citation: Duncan, G. J., Dowsett, C. J., Claessens, A., Magnuson, K., Huston, A. C., Klebanov, P., Pagani, L. S., Feinstein, L., Engel, M., Brooks-Gunn, J., Sexton, H., Duckworth, K., & Japel, C. (2007). School readiness and later achievement. Developmental Psychology, 43(6), 1428-1446. https://doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.43.6.1428
design: Secondary analysis of 6 longitudinal datasets with meta-analysis of coefficients; regressions with school-entry academic, attention and socioemotional skills entered together, most models controlling pre-school-entry cognitive, attention, socioemotional skills and family background
population_location: Six longitudinal datasets (US, UK, Canada per author list; countries not listed in abstract)
outcome: Later school reading and math achievement
effect_as_reported: School-entry math strongest, then reading, then attention; socioemotional behaviors generally insignificant; no coefficients in abstract
excerpt: By contrast, measures of socioemotional behaviors, including internalizing and externalizing problems and social skills, were generally insignificant predictors of later academic performance
note: Abstract: 'Across all 6 studies, the strongest predictors of later achievement are school-entry math, reading, and attention skills.' The control set is prior (pre-entry) skills plus the other school-entry skills; it does not adjust for a baseline of the later outcome at the same point. Claim wording matches.

correct_citation: Romano, E., Babchishin, L., Pagani, L. S., & Kohen, D. (2010). School readiness and later achievement: Replication and extension using a nationwide Canadian survey. Developmental Psychology, 46(5), 995-1007. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018880
design: Longitudinal survey secondary analysis (replication of Duncan et al. 2007 regression strategy); kindergarten predictors entered together
population_location: 1,521 children, National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY), Canada-wide; Study 2 adds Montreal (MLEPS)
outcome: Grade 3 math and reading (Study 1); grade 3 socioemotional outcomes (Study 2)
effect_as_reported: Math strongest predictor; literacy and mother-reported attention predicted later achievement; no coefficients in abstract
excerpt: (a) math skills were the strongest predictor of later achievement, (b) literacy and attention skills predicted later achievement, and (c) socioemotional behaviors did not significantly predict later school achievement.
note: Attention is mother-reported. With multiple imputation, some socioemotional behaviors (hyperactivity/impulsivity, prosocial, anxiety/depression) also predicted grade 3 math and reading.

correct_citation: Pagani, L. S., Fitzpatrick, C., Archambault, I., & Janosz, M. (2010). School readiness and later achievement: A French Canadian replication and extension. Developmental Psychology, 46(5), 984-994. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018881
design: Prospective longitudinal population-based cohort, regression replicating Duncan et al. 2007; extension adds motor skills and classroom engagement
population_location: Population-based sample of French-speaking children in Quebec, Canada; MLEPS as reference group (N not in abstract)
outcome: End-of-grade-2 math, reading and general achievement; classroom engagement
effect_as_reported: Kindergarten math coefficients largest, then attention skills, receptive language, attention problems, behavior; no numbers in abstract
excerpt: In the replication model, kindergarten cognitive and attention characteristics predicted achievement by the end of 2nd grade.
note: Pages 984-994 from Crossref. Fine motor skills added independent prediction.

correct_citation: McClelland, M. M., Acock, A. C., Piccinin, A., Rhea, S. A., & Stallings, M. C. (2013). Relations between preschool attention span-persistence and age 25 educational outcomes. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(2), 314-324. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2012.07.008
design: Longitudinal cohort; structural equation modeling controlling for age-7 achievement (prior achievement), adopted status, vocabulary, gender, maternal education; logistic regression for college completion
population_location: N = 430 adopted and non-adopted children, Colorado Adoption Project (Colorado, US)
outcome: Math and reading achievement at age 21; college completion by age 25
effect_as_reported: 1 SD higher age-4 attention span-persistence = 48.7% greater odds of completing college by 25
excerpt: children's age 4 attention span-persistence significantly predicted math and reading achievement at age 21 after controlling for achievement levels at age 7, adopted status, child vocabulary skills, gender, and maternal education level
note: Note the baseline is age-7 achievement, measured after the age-4 predictor, not a pre-predictor baseline. Small, non-representative sample.

correct_citation: Morgan, P. L., Farkas, G., Hillemeier, M. M., Pun, W. H., & Maczuga, S. (2019). Kindergarten children's executive functions predict their second-grade academic achievement and behavior. Child Development, 90(5), 1802-1816.
design: Longitudinal, nationally representative, multi-year autoregressive panel with domain-specific and domain-general autoregressors (prior achievement and behavior controlled)
outcome: Grade 2 reading, mathematics, science achievement; behavioral self-regulation; problem behaviors
effect_as_reported: Working memory effects .08 SD (science) to .12 SD (mathematics); some effects about .04 SD
excerpt: working memory's predictive relations with children's academic achievement ranged from .08 of a standard deviation for science achievement to .12 of a standard deviation for mathematics achievement
note: Existence, design and prior-achievement control confirmed. Effect range is looser than claimed: the paper gives .08-.12 SD for working memory; the '.05' lower bound was not found. Effects differ by EF type (cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control predict only some outcomes).

correct_citation: Duckworth, A. L., Quinn, P. D., & Tsukayama, E. (2012). What No Child Left Behind leaves behind: The roles of IQ and self-control in predicting standardized achievement test scores and report card grades. Journal of Educational Psychology, 104(2), 439-451.
design: Two prospective longitudinal studies; SEM controlling for prior test scores and prior grades plus demographics (plus a third teacher-survey study)
population_location: Study 1: NICHD SECCYD children from 10 US sites (grade 4 predictors, grades 8-9 outcomes); Study 2: N = 510 middle school students in two schools
outcome: Change in standardized achievement test scores and report card grades / GPA
effect_as_reported: Study 1: test-score change self-control beta = .01 (p = .88), grades beta = .20; Study 2: tests beta = -.05 (p = .43), GPA beta = .22 (p < .001)
excerpt: IQ (β = .12, p < .001) but not self-control (β = −.05, p = .43) predicted standardized achievement test scores when controlling for prior-year standardized achievement test scores.
note: Study 1 excerpt: test score changes 'predicted by IQ (β = .29, p < .001) but not self-control (β = .01, p = .88)'. Published 2012 (online 2011).

correct_citation: Magnuson, K., Duncan, G., Lee, Y.-G., & Metzger, M. (2009). Early school adjustment and high school dropout. Paper prepared for SRCD paper panel, April 2, 2009 (preliminary conference draft); posted by the Foundation for Child Development, 2011.
design: Secondary analysis of two longitudinal datasets; regressions adjusting for family and individual background, with academic skills and behaviors entered together; not a baseline-of-outcome design
population_location: US: children of NLSY (NLSY Child) and Baltimore Beginning School Study; skills and behaviors at age 7 or 8
outcome: High school completion, college attendance, completed years of schooling
effect_as_reported: Attention problems do not predict attainment; early skills and behaviors modestly and inconsistently predictive; no coefficients in abstract
excerpt: In contrast, attention problems do not predict adolescent and early-adult school attainment.
note: Finding matches, but the source is an unreviewed 2009 conference draft marked 'PRELIMINARY CONFERENCE DRAFT – DO NOT CITE OR QUOTE'; 2011 is the FCD posting date. Persistent attention problems before age 10 also did not predict attainment.
